claim: In most configurations an alias record can have the same name as the hosted zone (the zone apex), but a CNAME record cannot.
question: Can you create an alias record or a CNAME record at the zone apex?

values.display: you can create an alias record
You can't create a CNAME record

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 records at the zone apex
qualifiers.condition: For alias records, the exception is an alias at the apex that points to a CNAME record in the same hosted zone.

evidence.quote: In most configurations, you can create an alias record that has the same name as the hosted zone (the zone apex).
You can't create a CNAME record that has the same name as the hosted zone (the zone apex).

note: d13-017, d13-101. Callvale: the root domain needs an alias, not a CNAME.

claim: The one exception for an alias record at the zone apex is a redirect to a record of type CNAME in the same hosted zone; the alias record must have the same type as the record it routes to, and a CNAME record for the zone apex is not supported even for an alias record.
question: When can you not create an alias record at the zone apex?

values.display: a type of CNAME
must have the same type

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 alias record at the zone apex
qualifiers.condition: The alias target is a record in the same hosted zone.

evidence.quote: The one exception is when you want to redirect queries from the zone apex (such as example.com) to a record in the same hosted zone that has a type of CNAME (such as zenith.example.com).
The alias record must have the same type as the record you're routing traffic to, and creating a CNAME record for the zone apex isn't supported even for an alias record.

claim: An alias record can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources (the list includes S3 buckets, CloudFront distributions and another record in the same hosted zone), while a CNAME record can redirect DNS queries to any DNS record.
question: Where can an alias record send queries, compared with a CNAME record?

values.display: selected AWS resources
redirect DNS queries to any DNS record

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 alias and CNAME records
qualifiers.condition: The alias list is not limited to S3 buckets, CloudFront distributions and another record in the same hosted zone.

evidence.quote: An alias record can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources, including but not limited to the following:

Alias records let you route traffic to selected AWS resources, such as CloudFront distributions and Amazon S3 buckets. They also let you route traffic from one record in a hosted zone to another record.
A CNAME record can redirect DNS queries to any DNS record.

claim: With a CNAME record you do not need to use Amazon Route 53 as the DNS service for the domain you redirect queries to.
question: Must the target of a CNAME record be hosted in Route 53?

values.display: You don't need to use Route 53 as the DNS service

evidence.quote: You don't need to use Route 53 as the DNS service for the domain that you're redirecting queries to.

claim: Amazon Route 53 does not charge for alias queries to AWS resources, but it charges for CNAME queries.
question: Does Route 53 charge for alias queries and for CNAME queries?

values.display: doesn't charge for alias queries to AWS resources
charges for CNAME queries

qualifiers.condition: Alias queries are free when the alias target is an AWS resource.

evidence.quote: Route 53 doesn't charge for alias queries to AWS resources.
Route 53 charges for CNAME queries.

claim: A CNAME record that redirects to another record in a Route 53 hosted zone is charged as two queries per DNS query, because the resolver must send a second query for the record in the first response.
question: How many queries does Route 53 charge for a CNAME that points to another Route 53 record?

values.display: charged as two queries

qualifiers.scope: per DNS query to a CNAME record that redirects to a record in a Route 53 hosted zone
qualifiers.condition: The target record is in the same hosted zone or another Route 53 hosted zone.

evidence.quote: If you create a CNAME record that redirects to the name of another record in a Route 53 hosted zone (the same hosted zone or another hosted zone), each DNS query is charged as two queries:
If the CNAME record redirects to the name of a record that is hosted with another DNS service, Route 53 charges for one query.

claim: Amazon Route 53 answers a query for an alias record only when the name and the type of the alias record match the name and type in the query, while a CNAME record redirects queries for a record name whatever the record type in the query.
question: Does an alias record answer queries of any record type, like a CNAME does?

values.display: match the name and type in the DNS query
regardless of the record type specified in the DNS query

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 alias and CNAME records

evidence.quote: Route 53 responds to a DNS query only when the name of the alias record (such as acme.example.com) and the type of the alias record (such as A or AAAA) match the name and type in the DNS query.
A CNAME record redirects DNS queries for a record name regardless of the record type specified in the DNS query, such as A or AAAA.

claim: When an alias record points to an AWS resource, Amazon Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own; if the IP address of a load balancer behind an alias record changes, Route 53 answers queries with the new IP address.
question: What happens to an alias record when the IP address of its AWS target changes?

values.display: Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own
responding to DNS queries with the new IP address

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 alias record that points to an AWS resource

evidence.quote: When you use an alias record to route traffic to an AWS resource, Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own.
If the IP address of the load balancer changes, Route 53 starts responding to DNS queries with the new IP address.

note: d13-101, d13-102 (Ben: why not an A record at the IP address of the load balancer).

claim: For an alias record that points to an AWS resource you cannot set the TTL and Amazon Route 53 uses the default TTL of the resource; for an alias record that points to another record in the same hosted zone, Route 53 uses the TTL of the target record.
question: Can you set the TTL of an alias record?

values.display: you can't set the time to live (TTL)
Route 53 uses the TTL of the target record

qualifiers.condition: The TTL source depends on whether the alias target is an AWS resource or a record in the same hosted zone.

evidence.quote: If an alias record points to an AWS resource, you can't set the time to live (TTL); Route 53 uses the default TTL for the resource. If an alias record points to another record in the same hosted zone, Route 53 uses the TTL of the target record.

claim: An alias record that points to an ELB load balancer can be created both for the root domain, such as example.com, and for subdomains, such as www.example.com, which is a difference from a CNAME record.
question: Can an alias record to a load balancer be created for the root domain as well as for subdomains?

values.display: both for the root domain

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 alias record to an ELB load balancer

evidence.quote: It's similar to a CNAME record, but you can create an alias record both for the root domain, such as example.com, and for subdomains, such as www.example.com.

claim: Amazon Route 53 does not charge for alias queries to ELB load balancers or other AWS resources.
question: Does Route 53 charge for alias queries that point to a load balancer?

values.display: doesn't charge for alias queries to ELB load balancers

evidence.quote: Route 53 doesn't charge for alias queries to ELB load balancers or other AWS resources.

claim: As traffic changes, Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and updates its DNS entry, and that DNS entry specifies a time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds so the IP addresses can be remapped quickly.
question: Why do the IP addresses behind a load balancer DNS name change, and what TTL does its DNS entry use?

values.display: time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds
scales your load balancer and updates the DNS entry

evidence.quote: As traffic to your application changes over time, Elastic Load Balancing scales your load balancer and updates the DNS entry. The DNS entry also specifies the time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds. This helps ensure that the IP addresses can be remapped quickly in response to changing traffic.

note: d13-102: Ben asks why an A record cannot point at the load balancer IP address. Neighbour page (chapter 14 owns ELB).

claim: For a website on one EC2 instance, AWS recommends creating an Elastic IP address and associating it with the instance, because an Elastic IP address ensures that the IP address of the instance will never change.
question: How can you keep the IP address of a single EC2 instance stable behind a Route 53 record?

values.display: will never change

qualifiers.scope: Amazon EC2 instance behind a Route 53 record
qualifiers.condition: Pricing for Elastic IP addresses applies.

evidence.quote: We recommend that you also create an Elastic IP address and associate it with your EC2 instance. An Elastic IP address ensures that the IP address of your Amazon EC2 instance will never change.

note: d13-101. Callvale option 2 (Elastic IP on one instance).

claim: When several resources perform the same function and each record has a health check, Amazon Route 53 routes traffic away from the record whose underlying resource the health check finds unhealthy.
question: What does Route 53 do with a record whose health check reports the resource as unhealthy?

values.display: Route 53 routes traffic away from the associated record

qualifiers.condition: A health check is associated with each record for the resources that perform the same function.

evidence.quote: If a health check determines that the underlying resource is unhealthy, Route 53 routes traffic away from the associated record.

claim: For AWS resources that you can create alias records for, you should not create Route 53 health checks; you set Evaluate Target Health to Yes on the alias record instead.
question: How do you health check an AWS resource that has an alias record in a failover setup?

values.display: set Evaluate Target Health to Yes

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 failover configuration with alias records
qualifiers.condition: The resource is an AWS resource for which you can create alias records.

evidence.quote: If you're routing traffic to any AWS resources that you can create alias records for, don't create health checks for those resources. When you create the alias records, you set Evaluate Target Health to Yes instead.

note: d13-104. Callvale stage 4: primary alias to the ALB with Evaluate Target Health.
